::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 67 columns across 13 data files.
#### Issues Identified

4 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 13 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

text.text: Phonetic studies sometimes infer how many categories a linguistic system contains using surface distributional diagnostics.
This inference is examined by distinguishing four levels: distribution shape, labeled-group separation, statistical components, and linguistic categories.
In an equal-proportion, equal-variance Gaussian mixture, two speech categories produce a unimodal pooled distribution when the distance between their means is less than two standard deviations.
In many realistic contexts, unimodality of a pooled distribution alone does not establish the presence of a single linguistic category.
Conversely, bimodality of a pooled distribution alone does not establish two linguistic categories.
The standard mixture-variance decomposition also shows that a two-category mixture need not have greater variance than its more variable component.
Simulations show mode-based diagnostics can correctly describe surface modality yet poorly recover the categories that generated the data.

Empirical cases further illustrate that distribution shape, labeled-group separation, and component structure capture distinct properties of the data and need not converge on the same category analysis.
These diagnostics should thus be interpreted at their own levels.
Agreement among them can strengthen a description of surface structure, but they cannot determine categoryhood on their own.
Category-level claims require converging linguistic evidence suited to the category under study.

text.text: Some of this work also uses perceptual, social, or historical evidence, so it should not be characterized as relying on an acoustic statistic alone.
It nevertheless documents an operational step used to infer category structure from acoustic distributions.

An important inferential point to note here is that the technique presupposes a category distinction and uses acoustics-based measures to quantify the realization of the categories already supplied; it does not independently establish whether those categories remain distinct units in the linguistic system.
Notably, forward and reverse inferences have different evidential status.
Given a specified generating mechanism, we can derive or simulate the population densities it may produce.
The inverse is less determinate because the same surface pattern may be compatible with multiple generating mechanisms.
Quantitative classification research has long recognized that both the presence and the absence of bimodality admit multiple explanations (Murphy, 1964).

text.text: Distribution shape therefore describes the observed or estimated density, not the number of latent or linguistic categories.
Measures of labeled-group overlap or distance describe acoustic separation under labels whose status has already been assumed or established.

Previous work (Smith, Sonderegger, & The SPADE Consortium, 2024) has examined the limitations of these measures as estimates of separation, including their sensitivity to unbalanced data and the difficulty of quantifying their uncertainty; Stanley and Sneller (2023) show that sample size plays a critical role in interpreting Pillai scores.

text.text: However, even if the estimate of separation is reliable, the labeled groups do not necessarily correspond to distinct linguistic categories.
Mixture models have the same issue.
They estimate statistical components under specified distributional assumptions and selection criteria.
Their solutions represent the data statistically but do not directly establish linguistic categoryhood.
Near merger makes this cross-level problem especially clear.

Linguistic behavior can reveal distinctions that acoustic distance does not.

Other category claims may require evidence from lexical processing, perception, production, or sociolinguistic evaluation.
As far as possible, such evidence should be independent of the surface distributional measure being evaluated.
This avoids using the same acoustic measure both to establish and to validate the labels.
This paper examines what surface distributional diagnostics can support in category inference.

Distribution shape, labeled-group separation, and model-based component structure each answer a legitimate question, but problems arise when their outputs are treated as direct measures of linguistic categoryhood.
Modality provides the central formal example because its relation to population structure can be derived explicitly.

The contribution is methodological rather than mathematical: the paper integrates established distributional results, category-recovery simulations, and empirical cases within a single framework for evaluating cross-level inference.
Section 2 uses modality and variance to establish the formal problem.
Section 3 evaluates category recovery when the outputs of mode-based diagnostics and mixture models are interpreted as category number in finite samples.
Section 4 applies the same distinction to empirical cases.
Together, these analyses show how surface diagnostics can inform category analysis and why category-level claims require additional linguistic evidence.
2 Formal background 2.1 Modality Modality provides a clear example of the broader inferential problem.
A mode is a local maximum of a probability density function.

It is therefore a property of a surface distribution, whether the pooled population density or a density estimated from a sample, not a count of the component populations or linguistic category that generated it.
Nevertheless, a pooled distribution with one peak may be interpreted as evidence for one component population or category, while a distribution with two peaks may be interpreted as evidence for two.
Neither inference is generally valid.
We first consider the inference from one surface mode to one generating population.

The modality of a two-component normal mixture is an established result: it depends on the distance between the component means, the component variances, and the mixing proportions (Behboodian, 1970; Eisenberger, 1964). text.text: In linguistic data, two modes may well reflect two distinct populations of tokens, such as conditioned realizations of a single category, different speaker or task groups, or different measurement procedures, but these need not be the categories under investigation.
Bimodality can therefore motivate an analysis of possible sources, but on its own it cannot tell us whether the modes correspond to the linguistic categories we want to learn about.
The two errors are symmetrical.

Unimodality of the mixture distribution cannot rule out multiple independently established speech categories, and bimodality of the mixture distribution cannot establish multiple linguistic categories without evidence that the modes correspond to distinct units in the relevant linguistic system.
Modality constrains an account of category structure but does not uniquely identify it.

This condition is more likely to hold when the two conditional means are close, when the higher-variance speech category contributes a relatively small share of the pooled observations, or when the conditional variances differ greatly.
The result does not imply that pooling generally reduces variance.
It shows instead that a mixture need not have greater variance than each component population, even though its variance includes a non-negative betweenpopulation term.
Variance therefore places constraints on possible generating structures but does not uniquely identify them.
A pooled variance smaller than the larger category-conditioned variance is compatible with two independently established speech categories.

Section 3.2 examines how sampling variation affects this variance comparison in finite datasets.
The established result in Section 2.1 concerns population densities.
Under the equal-proportion and equal-variance assumptions, the relation between d and 2σ determines whether two speech categories produce one surface mode or two.

However, it is crucial to highlight that empirical analyses use finite samples, which introduce sampling variation and make the issue of inferring latent or linguistic categories that much harder than it is for abstract mixture populations.
In these samples, sampling variation can add local irregularities to a unimodal pooled density or hide weak separation in a bimodal pooled density.
The following simulations examine common diagnostics when the number of underlying speech categories is known but only the pooled acoustic observations are analyzed.
The simulations retain the idealized correspondence established in the formal example: two independently specified speech categories generate two Gaussian VOT populations.
The mixing proportion is fixed at p = 0.5, and the shared standard deviation at σ = 12.5.
The distance between the two conditional means, d, takes the values 10, 15, 20, 24, 26, 30, 35, and 40.
Since 2σ = 25, the pooled population density is unimodal when d < 25 and bimodal when d > 25.

For each value of d, we draw a pooled sample of 500 tokens and repeat the procedure 1,000 times.

Each sample is analyzed with four diagnostics: (i) peak counting on a kernel density estimate (KDE), (ii) Hartigan's Dip Test, (iii) Silverman's test, and (iv) a Gaussian mixture model (GMM) comparing one-and two-component solutions by BIC.
We evaluate these methods because they are commonly used to infer category structure from phonetic distributions.
The methods do not estimate the same statistical object: KDE peak counting and the mode tests concern surface modality, whereas GMM concerns statistical components under a specified model.
To compare them, we treat each output as an estimate of the number of underlying speech categories.

We define category-recovery accuracy, henceforth shortened to accuracy, as the proportion of replications in which this interpretation correctly recovers the two underlying speech categories used to generate the data.
For KDE, a replication is counted as accurate when exactly two local maxima are detected; one peak or three or more peaks do not recover the two categories.
For a formal mode test, it is counted as accurate when unimodality is rejected.
For GMM, it is counted as accurate when a two-component model is preferred.
This definition does not evaluate whether each method correctly answers its own statistical question.
A mode test may correctly identify the pooled population density as unimodal while being counted as inaccurate under the category-number interpretation.

Note that even in this idealized setting, where the underlying categories are known, mode-based diagnostics and mixture models cannot serve as standalone evidence for category number in empirical data.
The standard variance decomposition applied in Section 2.2 shows that variance magnitude does not map directly onto the number of underlying categories.
A mixture of two categoryconditioned populations may have variance either greater or smaller than its more variable component.
Conversely, a large surface variance can arise from heterogeneity within a single category.
Larger variance therefore does not establish more categories, and smaller variance does not establish fewer categories.

The simulation demonstrates one direction of the broader non-correspondence: two known speech categories do not necessarily produce a pooled variance greater than the larger conditional variance, and finite samples make this comparison less stable near the theoretical boundary.
The reverse inference is also unsupported.

A large variance may reflect separation between populations, but it may instead reflect variation among speakers, lexical items, phonological environments, tasks, or measurements within a single category.
Variance magnitude alone therefore cannot distinguish one category from multiple categories.
Like modality, variance can describe and constrain an account of a surface distribution, but it cannot determine category number.
A smaller pooled variance does not establish fewer categories, and a larger pooled variance does not establish more.
The relation can be summarized as follows: surface variance magnitude ̸ ⇒ number of generating populations ̸ ⇒ number of linguistic categories.
The preceding sections distinguished surface properties from category structure through formal examples and simulations.

The same distinction guides empirical analysis: distribution shape describes the modality of pooled observations, labeled-group metrics describe acoustic separation after labels have been assigned, and mixture models represent statistical components.
These diagnostics may fail to recover a distinction established on independent linguistic grounds or may identify surface structure that does not correspond to a category distinction.
The cases below illustrate both possibilities.

Measures such as Pillai's trace, Euclidean distance, and Bhattacharyya affinity answer this conditional question: given a set of labels, how strongly do the corresponding observations overlap or differ in the selected dimensions?
They do not establish the linguistic status of the labels.

Acoustic separation can support a description of labeled groups, but it cannot independently validate labels derived from that separation.
The magnitude of labeled-group distance is also conditional on the acoustic dimensions, sample size, and within-group variability.
A weak difference in one dimension may coexist with separation in another dimension or in a multivariate space.
It cannot establish that two independently motivated categories have merged.
Conversely, a large acoustic difference shows that the assigned groups are separated in the measured space, but it does not show that the groups function as distinct units in the linguistic system.
Labeled-group metrics evaluate the phonetic realization of labels; categoryhood requires evidence for the labels themselves.
A third evidential level concerns latent statistical components.

A Gaussian mixture model compares representations with different numbers of components under assumptions about the component distributions, their variances or covariances, and the model-selection criterion.
Its direct output is therefore a property of a fitted statistical model, not a count of linguistic categories.
In the simulations in Section 3.1, the speech categories and their one-to-one correspondence with Gaussian components are known by construction.
In empirical data, however, the relationship between statistical components and linguistic categories is not known in advance.
Multiple components may reflect conditioned realizations, speaker groups, styles, or measurement structure within one linguistic category.
Dillon, Dunbar, and Idsardi (2013) illustrate this problem with Inuktitut vowels, which are realized differently before uvular consonants.

A standard Gaussian mixture fitted to the acoustic data recovered the intended categories only unreliably, with the solution depending on the prior and the amount of data; the three phonemic categories were recovered more accurately when the model jointly learned the context-conditioned relation between allophones.
Thus, each phoneme corresponds not to a single Gaussian component but to linked, context-dependent distributions.
Conversely, one component may cover multiple categories when their acoustic distributions overlap or when the relevant distinction is realized in a dimension omitted from the model.
Model selection adds a further dependency.
AIC, AICc, BIC, and ICL may prefer different component structures because they balance fit, complexity, and component separation differently.
A one-component solution therefore cannot establish that a merger is complete, and a two-component solution cannot establish that two linguistic categories are present.
Mixture models can identify statistical heterogeneity and generate hypotheses about its sources.
The correspondence between a component and a linguistic unit must be demonstrated with evidence outside the component solution itself.
The preceding cases distinguish the existence of a category from the performance of a diagnostic.
This distinction is also central to earlier critiques of quantitative classification (Murphy, 1964).

Category-level claims instead require converging evidence suited to the type of category being proposed.
Phonological categories may be supported by patterning and alternations; and sociolinguistic categories by social evaluation, style-shifting, and community-level meaning.
As far as possible, this evidence should be independent of the surface distributional measure being evaluated.

text.text: These data provide a test case for surface diagnostics because the underlying voicing distinction is established by morphological alternations, independently of the acoustic measure.
The Dip Test results and density estimates reported here were computed from the original data without modification.
The acoustic difference is small relative to production variability.
In the pooled duration data illustrated in Figure 14, Hartigan's Dip Test does not reject unimodality (D = 0.0098, p = 0.8423).

text.text: This result addresses the modality of the pooled duration distribution.

At the same time, it shows that a distinction known to exist in the grammar can leave no detectable trace in surface modality: as with the Hillenbrand vowels, a researcher relying on modality alone would recover a single category where the grammar has two underlying categories.
Therefore, establishing such a distinction requires evidence from phonological patterning, lexical structure, processing, or other relevant behavior.
A duration distribution can provide evidence about phonetic implementation, but it cannot decide the underlying category analysis by itself.
Together, the empirical cases support interpreting distributional evidence at the level it directly addresses.
Surface shape, labeled-group separation, and model-based components constrain category analyses and identify patterns that require explanation.
Independent linguistic evidence supports the inference to categoryhood.
This paper examined cross-level inference from distribution shape, labeled-group separation, and model-based component structure to linguistic categoryhood.

Modality provides the clearest formal example: two independently specified speech categories can produce a unimodal pooled population density when their conditional means are sufficiently close, while bimodality does not identify the mechanism that generated the modes.
Variance exhibits the same non-correspondence.
A mixture variance is at least as large as the weighted average of the conditional variances but need not exceed the larger conditional variance.
Its magnitude therefore cannot determine category number.
The simulations evaluated the additional interpretation imposed when diagnostic outputs are treated as category number.
When d < 2σ, a mode test can correctly characterize the pooled population density as unimodal while showing low category-recovery accuracy.
text.formatted: When d < 2σ, a mode test can correctly characterize the pooled population density as unimodal while showing low category-recovery accuracy.

text.text: Near and above the boundary, test power, sampling variation, and bandwidth selection affect recovery.
GMM achieves higher accuracy under the simulated one-category-one-component correspondence, but that stipulated correspondence cannot be transferred to empirical data.
The simulated settings are more favorable than most linguistic datasets.
In both simulations, the observations follow Gaussian distributions, and each category corresponds to one Gaussian component.
In the modality simulations, the two categories also have equal proportions and conditional variances.
However, empirical data may contain unequal frequencies and variances, non-Gaussian distributions, and clustering by speaker, lexical item, phonological environment, or task.
These factors can alter surface shape and weaken the correspondence between statistical components and linguistic categories.
The diagnostics already have difficulty recovering known categories under favorable conditions.
They are therefore unlikely to perform better on empirical data.
The empirical cases are consistent with this expectation.

The Ness Gaelic case shows that the same generating parameters can yield different sampled patterns, and the Hillenbrand vowels show that established category distinctions may not produce detectable univariate bimodality.
The results support using each quantitative diagnostic at the level it directly addresses.
Mode tests evaluate surface modality.
Labeled-group metrics evaluate separation after labels have been assigned.
Mixture models compare component structures under particular distributional and selection assumptions.
Agreement among these methods may strengthen a description of surface structure.
However, it does not automatically strengthen a category-level claim because the methods do not provide independent evidence that the relevant modes, labels, or components are linguistic units.
This distinction is especially important in cases of near merger, incomplete neutralization, dialect contact, and category acquisition.
When acoustic distributions are close, surface evidence is less decisive even though the linguistic distinction may be theoretically important.
The appropriate response is not to abandon acoustic analysis, but to specify the inference that each result supports.

A category analysis should state what type of category is proposed, what the diagnostic directly estimates, how any labels were obtained, and whether the same measurement is being used both to define and validate those labels.
It should then identify the independent evidence that licenses a category-level interpretation and consider alternative mechanisms compatible with the observed surface pattern.
Independent category evidence must also be appropriate to the claim.
Phonological patterning and alternations can support phonological categories; and social evaluation, styleshifting, and community meaning can support sociolinguistic categories.
No single behavioral measure provides a universal criterion.

Stronger category inferences arise from converging evidence whose relation to the proposed category is explicit and which is, as far as possible, independent of the surface distributional measure under evaluation.
The formal results are deliberately simple.
The 2σ threshold applies to a one-dimensional mixture of two Gaussian populations with equal proportions and equal variances, and the simulations also only use a single acoustic dimension.
Multivariate analyses may change both surface shape and diagnostic performance.
As noted above, however, the other simplifying assumptions of the simulations favor the diagnostics rather than weaken the argument.
The empirical cases also concern different kinds of linguistic distinction.
A phonological category, a lexical representation, a dialect category, and a socially meaningful variant do not require identical validation criteria.
The purpose of comparing these cases is not to propose a single test for categoryhood, but to show why evidence must be matched to the category claim.

The present argument therefore limits the interpretation of surface diagnostics; it does not show that mode tests, labeled-group metrics, or mixture models are invalid for the statistical questions they directly address.
Surface distributional diagnostics provide useful descriptions and constraints.
They can identify modes, measure labeled-group separation, and compare statistical component structures.
By themselves, however, they cannot determine whether a linguistic contrast has been retained, lost, or reorganized.
What is needed is not less quantitative analysis, but a clearer account of what each analysis measures and what additional evidence supports the move to categoryhood.
We infer linguistic categories from how forms function in the linguistic system.
Surface distributions contribute to that inference rather than determine it.
